title: Petra and the Inheritance
premise: Estate lawyer Wren Ishikawa, who has quietly untangled three deaths the police ruled accidental, is hired to read the will of reclusive glassmaker Odile Marchetti—only to discover a second will, dated after the first and postmarked the day of the funeral, confessing to a murder no one reported. The confession points to a coded ledger hidden in the estate's stained-glass windows that names a killer still protected by a powerful local family. As the statute of limitations closes in, Wren must decode the ledger with an unlikely found family of Marchetti's estranged heirs before the killer silences them all. In the end, Wren exposes the truth at a public reading of the will, trading her invisibility for justice—and for the family she never meant to keep.
about_author: Elodie Voss spent a decade as a probate paralegal in coastal Oregon before turning to fiction, where her fascination with wills, secrets, and the paperwork of dying became her signature. She writes mysteries about people who fix what institutions won't.

chapters.title: The Second Will
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Three days after Odile Marchetti's funeral, Wren opens the estate file and finds a sealed envelope postmarked the day after death: a handwritten confession to killing 'the boy at the quarry' in 1979. The letter names no victim the police ever recorded. Emotional beat: cold dread beneath professional calm.

chapters.title: Invisible by Design
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, with flashback. We learn how Wren solved three prior 'accidents' without credit, feeding anonymous tips to a tired detective named Ruiz. Her rule: never be seen solving anything. The confession threatens that rule because it's addressed to her by name. Beat: the cost of invisibility.

chapters.title: The Glass House
chapters.summary: Wren visits the Marchetti estate, a cliffside house whose windows are Odile's own art. The named heirs—a disgraced chef, a teenage runaway, and a retired nun—are already circling, hostile to each other. One window depicts a quarry. Beat: unease; the house itself feels like testimony.

chapters.title: Heirs and Liars
chapters.summary: Alternating POV among the three heirs as they gather for the will reading. Chef Marco owes money; teen Juno ran from a group home; Sister Agnes hasn't spoken to Odile in thirty years. Each hides a connection to the dead woman. Beat: friction masking grief.

chapters.title: Reading Number One
chapters.summary: Wren reads the official will: everything to a foundation that doesn't exist. The heirs erupt. Privately, Wren realizes the foundation's registration date matches the quarry death. Beat: the legal puzzle snaps into focus.

chapters.title: The Quarry File
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She pulls 1979 records: a drowned boy, Danny Okafor, ruled accidental, case closed in nine days. His mother still lives in town and insists her son couldn't swim but never went near water alone. Beat: righteous anger kindles.

chapters.title: Ruiz's Warning
chapters.summary: Detective Ruiz POV. He recognizes Wren's fingerprints on the inquiry and warns her off—the Okafor case touches the Calloway family, who own half the county. First hint someone is watching Wren. Beat: fear arrives wearing a friendly face.

chapters.title: Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. Skipping school in the glass house, Juno notices the quarry window's panes are numbered like accounting columns. She photographs it. When she shows Wren, they realize Odile encoded a financial ledger across twelve windows. Beat: wonder and alliance.

chapters.title: The Calloway Angle
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The decoded entries trace payments from Calloway Development to Odile for decades—hush money. The final entry, dated two weeks before Odile's death, says only 'HE SAW ME.' Beat: stakes escalate from past crime to present danger.

chapters.title: Break-In
chapters.summary: Marco's POV. Someone ransacks the glass house overnight; the quarry window is cracked. Marco, who stayed late drinking, glimpses a figure in a Calloway Land Survey jacket. He tells no one, ashamed. Beat: guilt compounding silence.

chapters.title: Agnes Breaks Silence
chapters.summary: Sister Agnes POV. She finally reveals Odile's secret: in 1979 Odile witnessed Calloway patriarch Gerald kill Danny, and was paid to forget. Agnes chose the convent to escape being made complicit. Beat: catharsis; the found family deepens.

chapters.title: The Statute Clock
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Legal reality check: civil claims expire in weeks; criminal prosecution may be barred entirely. Justice outside the law becomes the only path—public exposure via the will itself. Beat: resolve hardens into strategy.

chapters.title: Danny's Mother
chapters.summary: Ruth Okafor POV. Wren visits Ruth, expecting to deliver closure; instead Ruth gives Wren Danny's sketchbook, full of drawings of the quarry—and one of a man's face. Beat: grief shared becomes fuel.

chapters.title: The Face in the Glass
chapters.summary: Juno and Wren compare the sketchbook portrait to the windows: the man is not old Gerald Calloway but his son, Richard—now the county judge. The confession letter's handwriting analysis suggests Odile wrote it under duress. Beat: vertigo; the law itself is the suspect.

chapters.title: Tail Lights
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren's car is run off a coastal road; she survives, staged to look like the same kind of accident she's debunked three times. Ruiz admits he's been ordered to bury the file. Beat: isolation; Wren can no longer stay invisible safely.

chapters.title: Found Family, Forged Plan
chapters.summary: All four POVs converge in the glass house. The heirs—strangers a week ago—agree to finish Odile's work together: fully decode all twelve windows before Richard can contest the estate. Beat: warmth against danger; the theme lands.

chapters.title: The Twelfth Window
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. The final window decodes to a complete account: every payment, dated, signed with Richard's childhood nickname only Odile would know. They photograph everything and hide copies. That night, the studio burns. Beat: triumph curdling to loss.

chapters.title: Ashes and Copies
chapters.summary: Marco's POV. The fire destroys the original windows but the heirs' off-site copies survive. Marco comes clean about the break-in witness; his honesty cements trust. Ruiz, moved past fear, agrees to receive the evidence publicly this time. Beat: redemption through confession.

chapters.title: Contested
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Richard files to invalidate the will and have Wren disbarred on fabricated ethics charges. A hearing looms where he'll be both accuser and, informally, arbiter. Beat: the trap closing; Wren gambles everything on one move.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Climax, Wren's POV. At the public will reading, Wren reads Odile's confession aloud, presents the ledger, Danny's sketchbook, and Ruth Okafor's testimony, with Ruiz standing witness. Richard's composure cracks when the childhood nickname appears. State investigators, tipped anonymously, are in the room. Beat: cathartic exposure.

chapters.title: What the Law Couldn't Hold
chapters.summary: Aftermath, multiple POVs. Richard is indicted; the ethics complaint collapses; the statute question becomes moot. Odile's estate funds a scholarship in Danny Okafor's name, administered by the three heirs. Beat: justice beyond verdicts; grief given somewhere to go.

chapters.title: Petra and the Inheritance
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue. Wren learns 'Petra' was Odile's private name for anyone who keeps watch over stone and glass and memory—she'd left Wren the title in a final letter. No longer invisible, Wren takes on a new impossible case, the heirs at her side. Beat: quiet hope; the family endures.
